How does Git help trace changes to a SQL database project?
column2:
Commits record the project's version history.
A commit records a snapshot and links it to earlier work. Its diff shows which SQL definitions changed, so reviewers can trace a schema change to the commit that introduced it.
Review source

column1: Why put each table, view, or procedure in its own SQL project file for Git review?
column2:
It makes object-level changes easier to review in Git diffs.
With one object per file, the file path identifies what changed before you read the diff. Separate files also let reviewers focus on a table or procedure without sorting through unrelated definitions.
Review source

column1: How can you organize SQL project folders so developers can find a table, view, or procedure?
column2:
Group files by object type, such as Tables, Views, and StoredProcedures.
Object-type folders give the team a predictable place to find a definition. For example, look under Views for a view rather than searching through a single file containing every object.
Review source

column1: Why exclude generated .dacpac build outputs from the source repository?
column2:
The build recreates them from the versioned project source.
A DACPAC is a generated database deployment package. Build it from the committed source and store the result as a pipeline artifact. Version the inputs so reviewers can see what produced it.
Review source

column1: What kinds of lookup values count as reference data in a SQL deployment?
column2:
Application lookup values, such as status codes or region lists.
Reference data contains controlled values the application relies on, such as a status ID for Shipped. An individual order is transaction data. Its status can refer to a reference row.
Review source

column1: Why version reference data scripts alongside the database schema?
column2:
To deploy required lookup values consistently with the schema that uses them.
The same commit can define a lookup table and supply the values the application expects in it. Creating the table alone does not insert those values. Version both so environments receive a consistent setup.
Review source

column1: When does a SQL project's pre-deployment script run relative to the planned schema changes?
column2:
Before the generated deployment plan executes.
The pre-deployment script runs before the planned schema changes execute. Use it for work that needs the old schema. The deployment tool already calculated the plan by this point.
Review source

column1: Which deployment script normally populates lookup tables after their schema changes?
column2:
The post-deployment script.
The post-deployment script runs after planned schema updates, so it can insert lookup values into a newly created table. It can run on later publishes too, so make its changes safe to repeat.
Review source

column1: How many entry files can a .sqlproj declare for each deployment script type?
column2:
At most one of each.
Each script type has one optional starting file. Use SQLCMD includes to pull in smaller files in the required order, rather than declaring a separate project entry for each seed file.
Review source

column1: When is the deployment plan calculated relative to the pre-deployment script?
column2:
Before the pre-deployment script executes.
SqlPackage calculates the plan from the source model and the target schema before it runs the pre-deployment script. Changing the schema in that script does not automatically make SqlPackage recalculate the plan.
Review source

column1: Why exclude seed files included via SQLCMD :r from the compiled SQL project model?
column2:
They contain deployment-time data statements rather than declarative schema definitions.
A seed file can contain INSERT or UPDATE statements that belong at deployment time. Excluding it from model compilation does not remove it from the deployment script if the entry file includes it.
Review source

column1: How can you see the actual SQL packaged from all the deployment script includes in a DACPAC?
column2:
Open a copy as a ZIP archive and inspect the packaged .sql scripts.
The package is an archive that contains the compiled schema and deployment scripts. Inspect a ZIP copy to see the combined SQL and make sure the included files appear in the intended order.
Review source

column1: What must happen to the intended lookup data when you run an idempotent seed script twice?
column2:
Rerunning it preserves the intended data state without introducing duplicate rows.
Idempotent means safe to repeat without changing the intended result. Match on a stable key so a second run updates an existing lookup row instead of adding another copy.
Review source

column1: What happens when multiple MERGE source rows match one target row for UPDATE?
column2:
SQL Server raises an error.
MERGE cannot update the same target row more than once in one statement. If two seed rows share the matching key and both match the target, the operation fails. Keep the source key unique.
Review source

column1: A seed MERGE is safe to rerun. Why test two deployments that run at the same time?
column2:
Concurrent executions can race or conflict when inserting or updating keys.
Idempotence describes runs that happen one after another. Two simultaneous runs can both try to insert the same missing key. Test that overlap separately rather than relying on a successful second run.
Review source

column1: A lookup row exists only in the target. What happens if MERGE has no WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE?
column2:
That MERGE specifies no action for those rows.
This MERGE only acts on matches or rows supplied by the source. If a target status is absent from the source list, the statement leaves it alone without a target-only action.
Review source
